newsitem.title: USA: Dun & Bradstreet targets minority, women-owned firms.
newsitem.headline: Dun & Bradstreet targets minority, women-owned firms.

text.p: Dun & Bradstreet Monday announced the formation of a specialised unit aimed at businesses owned by minorities and women, which it said would help fledgling entrepreneurs in two of the fastest-growing small business segments.

The provider of commercial credit and business marketing information said companies joining its Minority & Women-Owned Business Development Group would also be listed in its credit and marketing databases at no charge.
It said a listing in its marketing database would afford the following benefits, among others:
-- Increased visibility among D&B's contract customers, who check the database for potential suppliers, vendors, customers and partners.
-- Eligibility to bid on government contracts and engage in electronic commerce once they are assigned a DUN's number, an identification code assigned to 43 million businesses world-wide.
-- Increased access to capital, long-term financing and credit, once a company has provided the necessary information to institutions and vendors.
"Our traditional customers are trying to reach those small business customers," said Ron Wessin, who will head the group. "There is no national database of such businesses.
"When you identify your business as a minority- or woman-owned business, we list it in our marketing file, not our credit file," said Wessin. "A lot of companies are looking for such businesses."
He noted that many companies bidding on federal or state government projects do not know that they require a DUN's number. "They find that out when they apply for a state or federal job or a loan."

Companies receive the number when they list their business with the Murray Hill, N.J., company. D&B charges customers who buy information from it, but there is no charge for businesses to be listed with the 156-year-old firm.

A recent D&B survey of small business owners found that nearly half of the more than eight million women-owned businesses cannot afford to pay health care benefits to their employees. The survey also showed that 2.1 million minority-owned businesses have great difficulty in acquiring loans and in collecting debts owed them.

"Our studies show that small business owners, particularly women and minorities, are increasingly optimistic about their ability to grow now more than ever before," said George Martin, D&B executive vice president for mass marketing. "However, as relative newcomers to business ownership, women and minorities have their own distinct sets of challenges to overcome."
